item.title: As Computers Take the Driver’s Seat, Experts Worry About Safety
item.description:
Car software that does much of the work of driving is becoming more capable by the week. But, strangely enough, the better the technology becomes at steering, braking and navigating, the riskier it may be at least some of the time.

Experts call it automation complacency. In other words, drivers may overestimate what the technology can do and become so reliant on it that they stop paying attention and are unprepared when something goes wrong.

That happened recently to Kyle Shanahan, the head coach of the San Francisco 49ers, who has used the self-driving features of his Tesla for years. He dropped his cellphone while driving in Palo Alto, Calif., and bent over to pick it up, thinking that the technology would keep the car on a safe path.

But apparently the system, which relies on cameras, was not engaged, Mr. Shanahan told reporters in August. His car veered into oncoming traffic, causing a crash that left him with broken bones and a concussion.

One lesson Mr. Shanahan learned was that driving “is a partnership,” he told the reporters. “You don’t just turn it over to a computer.”

Most automakers are working on systems that, under certain conditions, steer and brake. Their ultimate aim is to sell fully autonomous vehicles that can act as robot chauffeurs so good that passengers will be able to read, work or fall asleep.

This month, Tesla began offering paid rides in a vehicle it calls the Cybercab, which has no steering wheel or brake pedals. Tesla says the Cybercab can operate without a driver. But it is not yet legal for carmakers to sell such vehicles to individuals.

Self-driving technology has won support from the Trump administration, in part because Chinese companies are also working on autonomous cars. Administration officials have said they are working on new rules to allow models like the Cybercab to hit the roads in large numbers.

Automated driving features have become sought-after options and a significant source of revenue for carmakers. Tesla charges $99 a month for its Full Self-Driving (Supervised) service. The company said it had 1.5 million active subscriptions in the second quarter, up from fewer than one million a year earlier.

Rivian, General Motors, Ford Motor, Hyundai and others are developing their own technology in what Ann Carlson, a former federal auto safety regulator, called an “arms race.”

But none of these systems available are designed to drive cars fully on their own. Unlike driverless taxis operated by Waymo and other companies, they require drivers to be ready to intervene if the software makes a mistake. In most circumstances, drivers, not car companies, are liable for accidents. And no comprehensive studies have shown that cars with automated features are safer than conventional vehicles, experts say.

“There is this irony,” said Ms. Carlson, who is now a professor at the U.C.L.A. School of Law. “The better it gets, in some respects the more dangerous it gets, unless it’s so good that it doesn’t cause problems, which is not true at this point.”

Guy Mangiamele, director of AMCI Testing, a research firm that evaluates vehicle technology, said Tesla had made “amazing” progress with its software, which is designed to guide vehicles to their destination with little or no human intervention.

Even so, “maybe it will take 500 miles or 1,000 miles, but at some point it’s going to get something wrong,” Mr. Mangiamele added. “If you’re not 100 percent aware and ready to take control, you’re going to be a danger to yourself and others around you.”

Notwithstanding those concerns, many people are embracing the technology.

Carolyn McBride of Oceanside, Calif., bought a Tesla Model Y last year after being wowed by the company’s self-driving technology. She did so, she said, despite her antipathy toward the right-wing views of the company’s chief executive, Elon Musk.

Ms. McBride, 72, said that she has trouble seeing in darkness and that her husband has Parkinson’s disease. The Tesla once prevented her from hitting a pedestrian, she said.

“It’s just such a game changer with people our age,” Ms. McBride said. The system is quick to warn her if she stops paying attention, she added.

Tesla recently described its self-driving technology as “a guardian angel for you & others on the road” in a post on X, Mr. Musk’s social media site. The company reposted a testimonial by a man who has cerebral palsy and said Full Self-Driving (Supervised) allowed him to go wherever he wanted, whenever he wanted.

Experts say claims like that are dangerous. “Partial automation requires a fully competent driver at all times,” said Alexandra Mueller, a senior research scientist at the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety, a research organization created by insurance companies. “Partial automation is not meant to compensate for impairments.”

Tesla did not respond to a request for comment.

People who rely on driver-assistance systems may not understand that they are usually liable for damage or injuries even when the vehicle was steering itself. Except in a few cases, the legal system has not penalized carmakers if something goes wrong, said Matthew Wansley, a professor at Cardozo School of Law in New York who studies automated driving.

Other automakers, including Ford, G.M. and Rivian, offer systems that are more cautious than Tesla’s. Such systems allow drivers to take their hands off the steering wheel on certain highways. The cars use cameras to monitor drivers and may sound alerts or automatically pull over if drivers are not attentive and responsive enough.

But it’s not clear how driver-assistance systems affect safety. Crash reports and statistics often do not contain information about whether such systems were engaged. Even the data that does exist may be misleading. That’s because cars with driver assistance systems tend to be more expensive, which means their owners are generally older, affluent people who are less accident prone.

Systems that clearly prevent injuries and fatalities tend to aid drivers by, among other things, sounding alarms or automatically braking a vehicle, rather than taking control from drivers, safety experts said. These experts consider hands-free driving systems and Tesla’s technology as more of a convenience than a safety feature.

“I have yet to see independent analyses confirming these significant benefit claims,” Dr. Mueller said.

Auto executives disagree, asserting that their systems make driving safer by making it less taxing.

“The biggest danger is actually drivers getting tired,” said James Philbin, senior vice president for autonomy and artificial intelligence at Rivian. “These systems can dramatically improve that.”

Rivian’s system allows drivers to take their hands off steering wheels on any road with clearly marked lanes. By the end of the year, the company plans to roll out technology that will allow cars to drive autonomously from point to point, similar to Tesla’s system. Drivers will still need to pay attention.

“Over time, the consumer expectation of what their vehicle can do is going to go up and up,” Mr. Philbin said. “And we want Rivian to be one of those top players.”

Other automakers have similar systems. Ford’s Blue Cruise and G.M.’s Super Cruise allow drivers to take their hands off the wheel on divided highways. The next step is cars that drive themselves from onramp to offramp.

“Basically you can get on the highway, you press a button and it’s going to do all the lane changes for you, all the interchanges, etc., all autonomously,” said Sammy Omari, executive director at Ford for advanced driver-assist systems.

In 2028, G.M. will begin equipping some vehicles with systems that allow drivers to take their eyes off the road. “Our goal is to get to full autonomy,” said Rashed Haq, vice president of autonomous vehicles at G.M.

But it is not clear when consumers will be able to buy cars that are so capable of driving that the person behind the wheel can completely check out.

Waymo has shown that driverless transportation is possible. But its vehicles operate in carefully mapped urban areas and are monitored by technicians.

Even when the technology is ready, not all consumers will be, said Olabisi Boyle, senior vice president of product planning for Hyundai Motor North America. “There’s still a significant majority that’s saying, ‘I need to trust this,’” she said, adding that acceptance will grow.

Mr. Musk has been predicting for more than a decade that fully autonomous vehicles were just around the corner. Mr. Philbin of Rivian estimates five years before consumers can buy a fully driverless vehicle, maybe less.

But Bryan Reimer, a research scientist in the M.I.T. Center for Transportation and Logistics, contends that those predictions are way too optimistic. “It’s decades,” he said, “not years.”

item.title: Trump Says He Supports Banning Diesel Exports to Bring Down Prices
item.description:
President Trump told reporters on Tuesday that his administration is reviewing a possible ban on U.S. exports of diesel to help lower fuel costs for farmers, truckers and businesses.

Some Republicans in Congress have been calling for a ban on exports as the cost of diesel has hit records because of global supply shortages that have resulted from the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran and the yearslong Russia-Ukraine conflict. The Iran war in particular, experts say, has driven much of the recent increase in diesel prices by reducing refining capacity.

Diesel fuel powers trains and trucks as well as large machinery and farm equipment. The record high prices for diesel means consumers ultimately pay more for food and other products. According to AAA motor club, the nationwide average diesel price was $6.53 a gallon on Tuesday, up from $3.69 a gallon a year ago.

“I’ve called for it,” Mr. Trump said about a ban on diesel exports. “I’ve called for it within my people. I’ve been talking about it.”

Rising energy costs have become an enormous political headache for the president as he tries to convince voters to elect Republicans in the November elections. Recent polls have shown many of the party’s candidates, including those running in what have long been regarded as safe Republican seats, in tight races with Democrats or independents.

Global demand for diesel fuel led to record-high exports from the United States this year, topping 1.6 million barrels a day in recent weeks, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Before the war started on Feb. 28, the country was exporting about 1.1 million barrels a day.

The E.I.A. this month said that it expected U.S. inventories of diesel to drop below 100 million barrels. Inventories reached a five-year low in 2025.

The American Petroleum Institute, which represents the country’s oil and natural gas industry, contends that a ban on U.S. exports of diesel would not bring relief to businesses and consumers. Instead, a ban would add to shortages by prompting U.S. refineries to reduce production, exacerbating the global shortage of the fuel.

The United States is currently the world’s largest supplier of diesel, providing about 20 percent of the eight million barrels of diesel traded by sea daily, the industry group said in a statement.

“Americans are hurting from rising diesel costs driven by an unprecedented disruption to global refining capacity,” Mike Sommers, president and chief executive at the petroleum institute, said in a statement. “We understand the administration is looking at every option to deliver relief, but restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem.”

Jim Mitchell, director of oil trading analytics at the research firm Wood Mackenzie, said Mr. Trump could use emergency powers to at least temporarily ban diesel exports. But doing so might not result a big immediate reduction in the price of the fuel.

“There is no switch that can make diesel prices go down in a week,” Mr. Mitchell said.

item.title: In Court Filing Defending Media Ban, White House Says Access Is a ‘Privilege’
item.description:
White House officials said in a court filing Tuesday that President Trump had determined that CNN, MS NOW and Politico had breached standards of conduct, leading to their expulsion from the White House grounds.

The alleged violations, said the filing, include “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information.”

“Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” reads the filing, which argues that Mr. Trump’s action against the three news outlets does not violate the First Amendment and aligns with a long history of presidents favoring some journalists over others.

The filing, furthermore, claims that the White House’s denial of access is a preliminary matter and that the outlets have until Friday to contest the decision.

The clash began last Friday, when Mr. Trump announced on Truth Social, the platform that he owns, that he would ban the three outlets, saying they “shouldn’t be able to constantly write or report FICTION and LIES.” On Saturday morning, journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied access to the White House grounds and had their press passes confiscated.

By Monday morning, the news organizations had sued, arguing that the president’s ban “brazenly discriminates based on editorial viewpoint,” and was an affront to their First Amendment rights. They said that the move had blindsided its targets, depriving the outlets of the warning that any such drastic action required. They “received zero advance notice that the president would ban a news organization from the White House if he dislikes its coverage,” according to the complaint.

U.S. District Judge Timothy J. Kelly, who was nominated in 2017 by Mr. Trump, will hold an emergency hearing on Wednesday to consider the media outlets’ request for a temporary court order undoing the access ban.

The government filing Tuesday night included copies of letters sent earlier in the day to each banned news outlet. In addition to accusing the organizations of failing to meet standards of conduct, the letters identified specific stories that allegedly either spread falsehoods or threatened national security. The letter to CNN, for example, cited a January 2026 story that “disclosed ‘top-secret’ construction details related to the East Wing bunker,” the letter reads.

One of MS NOW’s alleged infractions, according to a White House letter, was a June 2026 story claiming “a source said that President Trump ‘underestimated the willingness of Iran to resume conflict.’” Politico is accused of publishing a “document detailing funding for the White House ballroom containing intricate descriptions of how the Secret Service would invest in security improvements,” according to a White House letter.

The three media outlets did not immediately comment on the White House’s filing.

In their lawsuit, the media outlets argued that the White House hadn’t afforded them due process to contest their expulsion. In its response, the White House claims that it has provided the companies with “sufficient post-deprivation process.”

In 2018, Judge Kelly ruled against Mr. Trump in another media access case. Mr. Trump had expelled CNN reporter Jim Acosta from the White House grounds. But Judge Kelly ordered his credentials restored, saying Mr. Trump hadn’t given Mr. Acosta enough notice to challenge the action.

Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social last week that in light of Judge Kelly’s ruling in the Acosta case, the government would “almost without question” have to appeal the upcoming ruling.

Other news organizations have responded to the ban with acts of support and solidarity. The consortium of five TV networks that covers the president as the so-called TV pool — ABC News, CBS News, NBC News, Fox News and CNN — suspended its immersive coverage of Mr. Trump, and some news outlets temporarily withheld publication of photos of Mr. Trump’s events.

item.title: Trump Officials May Undo Nursing Home Mandates for Reporting Covid
item.description:
Nursing homes would no longer be required to report each week how many residents were stricken by Covid and other respiratory diseases, under a Trump administration plan to repeal a key public health response to thousands of pandemic deaths.

A draft summary of the proposed rule obtained by The New York Times outlines how the administration agrees with the industry’s objections to weekly reporting of viral caseloads, calling it burdensome. In its waning days, the Biden administration made Covid reporting rules permanent, adding influenza and respiratory syncytial virus (R.S.V.) to the list of threats that facilities also must track and record. The policy took effect in January 2025.

Advocates for nursing home residents reacted with dismay to the proposed rollback. Elderly, frail residents are especially vulnerable to infections, and they live in close quarters, where viruses can spread rapidly.

“That’s crazy,” said Sam Brooks, director of public policy at the nonprofit National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care. “We know, if anything, that respiratory disease has a disproportionate and deadly impact on nursing home residents.”

He said the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, or C.M.S., which regulates nursing homes, would be blinding itself to an important method for tracking infection control and pinpointing problems.

The administration has cut back on data updates at other agencies, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, where a study published this year found that databases related to vaccine and respiratory diseases had gone dormant.

Nursing home industry representatives declined to comment on specifics, because the changes have not been announced. They contend infection reporting consumes too much staff time and is duplicative, because infection data is reported to the federal government and states in other ways.

C.M.S., which drafted the plan, declined to discuss the proposal or disclose when it would be made public.

During the peak years of the pandemic, from early 2020 through early 2022, more than 200,000 nursing home residents and staff members died after being infected by coronavirus, according to KFF, an independent health policy organization, which cited C.D.C. data.

The high death toll has been attributed in part to a lack of preparedness and weak infection controls. The Government Accountability Office said in 2020 that inspectors had cited 82 percent of nursing homes for infection control deficiencies from 2013 to 2017, and that half of those were found to be repeat violators.

In the internal document obtained by The Times, Dr. Mehmet Oz, the director of C.M.S., recommended to his boss, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., that the agency pursue steps to undo the mandate.

“The agency does not comment on purported internal or pre-decisional deliberative materials,” a C.M.S. a spokesman said in an email. He said the agency evaluated regulations to ensure they “allow providers to focus time and resources on delivering care rather than unnecessary administrative burden.”

The draft memo from Dr. Oz to Mr. Kennedy said C.M.S. would reserve the power to reinstate weekly reporting if another public health emergency occurred.

The plan also would end a requirement that nursing home staffs be educated about Covid vaccines and offered the shots. Groups representing residents called the move unwise, pointing out that frontline caregivers were a key pathway for the coronavirus to enter nursing homes during the height of the pandemic. Covid vaccine rates among staff members in recent years have been below 10 percent, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported.

The administration plan would continue to mandate that facilities offer the Covid vaccine to residents.

The nursing home industry has already achieved its biggest goal of President Trump’s second term: After a heavy lobbying blitz, the administration last year scrapped Biden-era minimum staffing rules that were intended to improve resident care.

Biden officials, in pushing the staff minimums, had cited Covid deaths along with decades of concerns about poor care, including deaths from bedsores, falls and medication errors. But the Trump administration said too many nursing homes, especially in rural areas, could not find enough staff to satisfy the requirements. Many workers who care for the elderly are typically paid less than janitors and retail employees, and the work can be grueling.

With the proposed change on infection reporting, the administration anticipates favorable reaction from the industry, according to the draft memo.

Two main nursing home lobbying groups — the American Health Care Association and LeadingAge — reiterated their opposition to weekly respiratory infection reporting, saying that other government programs track Covid infections and that respiratory illnesses are reported to many local health departments.

“This outdated reporting requirement is only adding hours of unnecessary administrative tasks to caregivers each week” said Holly Harmon, the American Health Care Association’s senior vice president of quality, regulatory and clinical affairs. “It’s time to streamline public health reporting and put patients over paperwork.”

But industry critics contend that operators are failing to heed the lessons of the pandemic. With low staffing levels and high turnover, infection control efforts are most likely in line with the prepandemic patterns flagged by the G.A.O., said Toby Edelman, senior policy attorney at the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

“I don’t think there is any reason to believe they have beefed up what they are supposed to be doing,” Ms. Edelman said.

item.title: Bessent Mistakenly Failed to Report Holdings of JP Morgan Stock
item.description:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent failed to disclose at least $100,000 of his husband’s JP Morgan stock last year, triggering a review of his family’s finances by the Treasury Department’s Office of Inspector General, according to a filing with the Office of Government Ethics.

Instead of reporting the money as stock, the initial financial disclosure form that Mr. Bessent filed last year ahead of his confirmation indicated that the funds were cash in an undisclosed bank account. The funds were divested last July after the error was caught and Mr. Bessent paid a $200 late fee because the mistake was not reported in a timely matter, according to a note on the filing written by Mark Vetter, an ethics official in the Treasury Department.

A former hedge fund manager, Mr. Bessent last year reported having assets worth more than $700 million after being tapped to be President Trump’s Treasury secretary. His husband, John Freeman, is a former assistant district attorney in New York who later became general counsel of Bessent Capital, one of Mr. Bessent’s former funds. Mr. Freeman was appointed last July to serve on the American Battle Monuments Commission.

Mr. Bessent’s mishandling of his family’s financial divestment obligations were reported earlier by Politico.

It is the second time that the Treasury secretary failed to comply with the divestment requirements that cabinet officials face when assuming top government roles.

Last August, the ethics office alerted the Senate that Mr. Bessent was delinquent in selling his holdings of thousands of acres of North Dakota soybean farmland. The holdings represented a potential conflict of interest because Mr. Bessent was leading trade talks with China that involved negotiations over its purchases of American soybeans. Mr. Bessent divested the farmland holdings last December after requesting an extension.

Mr. Freeman’s JP Morgan stock would not necessarily pose a conflict of interest for Mr. Bessent, however the Treasury secretary does wield significant influence over the financial sector. This week, he held meetings with Chinese officials at the New York headquarters of JP Morgan Chase.

The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment.

In the filing, Mr. Vetter wrote that the Office of the Inspector General reviewed the situation and determined that there had been no “knowing violation” of the Ethics in Government Act. Mr. Vetter said that he agreed with that finding.

item.title: Fox News Finds Itself at Odds With Trump on Press Ban
item.description:
Fox News’s bond with President Trump is undeniable. Prime time stars like Sean Hannity and Jesse Watters cheerlead his policies, the president’s daughter-in-law hosts a weekly show on the network, and Fox’s founder, Rupert Murdoch, attended Mr. Trump’s nominating convention in 2024.

Nonetheless, this week Fox News has joined other networks in standing up for the rival media outlets that Mr. Trump decried as “fake” and banned from the White House — and two senior Fox journalists emerged as lead actors in the White House press corps’s standoff with the administration.

At a glance, it’s an unlikely position for Fox News, wrought in part by history and in part by sheer coincidence. And it’s confused some liberal Fox critics and caused some heartburn for Trump hard-liners.

So first, some facts.

Fox News is one of the five major networks — the others are ABC, CBS, CNN and NBC — that form the presidential TV pool, sharing the duties and costs of generating video footage of Mr. Trump’s everyday activities. When the president barred CNN, along with Politico and MS NOW, from the White House last week, the networks rebelled, refusing to film his daily public events until CNN was reinstated.

Fox News did not hesitate to go along with the plan. On Tuesday night, for instance, Fox was the scheduled pool crew for Mr. Trump’s Air Force One arrival at Joint Base Andrews, but it declined to film the event.

A Fox News spokeswoman referred an inquiry on Wednesday to a joint statement from the five networks, which Fox co-signed: “No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting.”

Inside Fox News this week, journalists have kept an eye on the past and the future, according to people with knowledge of its internal deliberations.

It was a big deal when Fox News joined the White House TV pool in the 1990s, back when the fledgling channel was seeking legitimacy in Washington. And in 2009, the pool came to Fox’s defense. When the Obama administration called the network “a wing of the Republican Party” and moved to bar it from a Treasury Department event, the other networks refused to participate until the Obama team relented and reinstated Fox.

The network is also aware that, theoretically, a future Democratic administration could try to ban Fox News the way Mr. Trump has barred CNN, the people said. So standing up for CNN now may benefit Fox later. That sentiment has been echoed by conservatives like Ari Fleischer, who served as press secretary to former President George W. Bush. “Don’t ban them,” Mr. Fleischer wrote on X. “Or one day they’ll ban us.”

Fox News has also supported the journalists who were effectively evicted from the Pentagon in March by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth as part of a series of moves aimed at drastically curtailing reporters’ access to the Defense Department. Mr. Hegseth, a former “Fox & Friends Weekend” host, has not appeared on Fox News in more than a year, even as other networks, like CBS, have repeatedly booked him. (The New York Times has sued over the Pentagon restrictions.)

It so happens that the current chair of the five-network pool group — a role that rotates every quarter — is Bryan Boughton, Fox News’s Washington bureau chief. So Mr. Boughton was the signatory on a note on Monday decreeing that “effective today, the TV pool will not be covering events designated as pool coverage of the president.”

It also happens that the current president of the White House Correspondents’ Association is Jacqui Heinrich, an anchor and senior correspondent at Fox News. So Ms. Heinrich is the name and face behind many public statements condemning Mr. Trump’s aggression toward the media and demanding his administration respect the rights of the free press.

Not every Fox viewer is pleased, with some right-wing accounts on social media blasting the network for its actions.

But Fox is not alone among conservative-friendly networks in standing up for the White House press corps. The right-wing channel Newsmax is opposed to Mr. Trump’s press ban, according to its chief executive, Christopher Ruddy.

“We hope the president reconsiders his decision, as this would set a bad precedent for all media, including conservative outlets like Newsmax,” Mr. Ruddy said in an interview. “Newsmax asked tough questions during both the Obama and Biden administrations, and at no point did anyone suggest that we might be banned.”

item.title: Disney’s Fired C.E.O. Returns to Settle Scores With Bob Iger
item.description:
Bob Chapek was fired as Disney’s chief executive in 2022 after less than three years in the job. A botched succession had metastasized into a corporate civil war.

Some of it was beyond his control, like Covid, which shut down its lucrative theme parks. Some of it was of his own making, like missteps with Wall Street and Disney’s bungled response to Florida’s “Don’t Say Gay” law.

But that is not how he explains his downfall.

In a memoir set to be published Tuesday by Gallery Books, Mr. Chapek rejects any personal responsibility for his ouster. He places all blame on a “relentless” sabotage campaign by the man who handpicked him for the job, his predecessor and eventual successor, Robert A. Iger.

“My abrupt dismissal hurt my reputation, leaving those close to me, outsiders and some within the kingdom trying to figure out what I did wrong,” Mr. Chapek writes. “The answer, again, is nothing.”

Mr. Chapek uses “Behind the Castle Walls: My Thirty Years at the Happiest Place on Earth,” a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, to re-establish himself as a leader. He proudly embraces the mantle of “disrupter,” invoking the word or versions of it 30 times across 254 pages. He also seeks to reclaim a place in Disney history, writing that “my legacy wasn’t memorialized in a positive way.”

But Mr. Iger is the central preoccupation.

A spokesman for Mr. Iger declined to comment.

Here is what, specifically, Mr. Chapek claims that his former mentor did, along with some other things he wants readers to know.

The feud between the two Bobs is old news. Mr. Iger’s private criticism of his successor — and Mr. Chapek’s belief that Mr. Iger was undermining him — has been extensively reported.

But now Mr. Chapek is making the case himself, writing that Mr. Iger played “an intentional and preconceived role in abruptly ending my ride as Disney C.E.O.” Mr. Chapek says Mr. Iger disparaged him in private conversations, telling Hollywood power brokers and loyalists in the Disney ranks that he had shut Mr. Iger out and questioning his judgment over pandemic-era movie releases.

Mr. Chapek portrays Mr. Iger as manipulative and egotistic, someone who maneuvered to preserve his own authority after stepping down and then ultimately seized back the top job.

“I didn’t get a chance to finish what I started,” Mr. Chapek writes. “In truth, it pisses me off.”

Mr. Iger shocked Hollywood in February 2020 when he abruptly stepped down after 15 years as chief executive. The speed has remained a lingering question.

Mr. Iger has said he was tired of aspects of the job, notably earnings calls. And he did not exactly disappear: He remained for two years as executive chairman, with oversight of creative matters.

But Mr. Chapek floats a more conspiratorial explanation. “I have been told by several high-ranking people both in government and private business that in their opinions, the real reason he left the company so abruptly was his anticipation of the arrival of Covid,” Mr. Chapek writes.

He offers no evidence. Mr. Chapek also suggests that Mr. Iger believed he could reclaim the job whenever he wanted. (Disney has previously denied that the Covid-19 pandemic had anything to do with Mr. Iger’s decision.)

While running Disney’s theme park division and, later, serving as chief executive, Mr. Chapek faced criticism that he had taken his drive for higher revenue too far. Under his watch, the company sharply raised prices for annual park passes and food, and began charging for things that had once been free, including access to shorter lines and parking at Disney hotels in Florida.

He offers no mea culpa.

Mr. Chapek proudly recounts bringing airline-style dynamic pricing to Disney’s parks and argues that higher prices helped reduce crowding and increase guest satisfaction. “We’d been, at a minimum, leaving revenue opportunities on the table to avoid stirring the hornet’s nest,” he writes, pointing to 18 percent compound annual profit growth during his tenure as parks chairman.

In February, Disney named a new chief executive: Josh D’Amaro, a company veteran who once worked for Mr. Chapek in theme parks. In Mr. Chapek’s telling, Mr. D’Amaro was a protégé, “the tip of my spear” in all that disrupting.

“I consistently suggested the idea of promoting him,” Mr. Chapek writes. “He had been a relative unknown in the corporate hierarchy before I singled him out.”

A spokesman for Mr. D’Amaro declined to comment.

Repeatedly, Mr. Chapek returns to his core identity — a “square” machinist’s son from Indiana who was underestimated by Hollywood insiders but saw business opportunities that they missed. Recounting his push in the 1990s for Disney to make direct-to-video animated sequels, he writes: “It was Bob from flyover Indiana, educated at a state school, who disrupted the business and kept the studio afloat with an endeavor others had dismissed as ‘creative heresy.’”

item.title: Bond Yields Make Biggest One-Day Jump Since Trump’s Tariffs Rattled Markets
item.description:
Government bond yields rose sharply on Wednesday, fueled by stronger-than-expected manufacturing data that suggested the economy may be heating up faster than predicted, putting new pressure on the Federal Reserve to raise rates again.

The yield on 10-year notes, which underpins corporate and consumer borrowing across the globe, rose roughly 0.2 percentage points to around 5.1 percent, its biggest one-day jump since the immediate aftermath of President Trump’s “liberation day” tariff proposal, and its highest outright yield since the buildup to the global financial crisis. The five-year Treasury yield also rose above 5 percent, to its highest since 2007.

The rise in yields also weighed on the equity market, with the S&P 500 falling roughly half a percent on Wednesday after trading close to its record high at the start of the week.

Wednesday’s big move higher in yields comes during a period of turmoil in the bond markets. Earlier this month, the 10-year Treasury yield surpassed 5 percent for the first time in many years, a breach of a symbolic threshold that reflected investors’ unease with inflation, government deficits and booming spending on artificial intelligence.

Wednesday’s moves also extended months of rising yields around the world. The 10-year Treasury has risen more than a percentage point since the onset of the war with Iran, pushing up mortgage and other borrowing rates.

In Britain, comparable 10-year gilt yields have risen by a similar amount over the same period. French and Italian yields have risen even more.

The rise in U.S. yields has been partly spurred by persistent inflation stemming from increasing oil prices amid the simmering war in the Middle East.

But the increase has largely been driven by higher growth expectations tied to the expansion of artificial intelligence. Investors still worry that the demand for supplies and labor to complete the build-out of A.I. infrastructure could also feed into rising prices unless the Federal Reserve continues to raise interest rates.

On Wednesday, a monthly survey of executives at private companies by S&P Global showed stronger-than-expected manufacturing and services activity. But that strength of demand was accompanied with a warning that the surge of activity had started to push prices higher, threatening the inflation outlook.

Last week, the Federal Reserve raised rates a quarter of a percentage point, to a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent, citing the need to counter inflation. It was the first increase in rates in more than three years.

After the release of the manufacturing survey on Wednesday, investors raised their expectations that the Fed would increase interest rates again next month to a roughly 75 percent chance, up from 53 percent on Tuesday. The probability is derived from prices in interest rate futures markets, which allow investors to bet on the level of interest rates going forward.

Amid sharply rising yields, there was less-than-usual demand from investors to buy the five-year Treasuries at a government auction on Wednesday.

The tepid auction results point to the pros and cons of the recent rise in interest rates. With solid growth expected for years to come, some analysts have argued that Treasury yields should remain elevated, reflecting the strength of the economy. And those higher yield rates are typically attractive to investors.

But those higher yields are causing consternation for other reasons. Higher Treasury yields correspond to higher interest payments for the government on its $32 trillion debt pile, and for companies and consumers, many of them already struggling to keep up with rising prices and slowing wage growth.

item.title: Florida Files Lawsuit Against The New York Times
item.description:
Florida’s attorney general on Wednesday filed a shareholder lawsuit against The New York Times Company, claiming that the board of directors’ lack of oversight of the paper’s editorial practices is hurting state pension holders who have stock in the company.

The attorney general, James Uthmeier, said at a news conference in Doral, Fla., that the outlet’s credibility had been hurt in particular by what he saw as an anti-Israel bias in its coverage of the Israel-Hamas war.

The lawsuit demanded access to internal documents in an attempt to determine whether the company’s board of directors had allowed journalistic standards to be “weaponized within the company to serve the personal agendas of unchecked editors.”

Mr. Uthmeier said at the news conference that this legal filing was not a defamation suit, but a case about a company’s duties to shareholders.

“When you’re a news agency, your credibility is everything,” he said. “The New York Times tells its own investors that its brand and reputation are its most important assets.”

Charlie Stadtlander, a spokesman for The Times, said in a statement that the company would defend itself vigorously.

“This lawsuit has no merit and was brought for an improper purpose,” he said. “Although it is positioned as a corporate governance petition to inspect the company’s books and records, it is a transparent attempt to exert agenda-driven pressure against an independent media organization, level false allegations of bias and chill journalism protected by the First Amendment.”

The lawsuit was jointly filed in New York County Supreme Court by the State Board of Administration of Florida, which oversees Florida’s pension fund, and the National Center for Public Policy Research, a conservative think tank. According to the fund’s most recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission, Florida holds about 145,000 shares of Times stock.

The legal filing included reports from a person, identified in the filing as a former Times newsroom employee, who said she had raised concerns about anti-Israel bias in coverage of the Israel-Hamas war on numerous occasions and felt that the company’s internal mechanisms for standards had failed.

The announcement comes as Mr. Uthmeier, a Republican, runs to retain his seat as attorney general. Ron DeSantis, the Republican governor of Florida, appointed Mr. Uthmeier to the role in 2025.

As attorney general, Mr. Uthmeier has emerged as an aggressive conservative culture warrior, frequently holding news conferences to announce investigations or lawsuits against companies or institutions. This week, his office announced a settlement with Starbucks after suing the company, accusing it of violating a state anti-discrimination law by favoring the hiring of minorities.

He has also opened investigations into the National Football League over practices encouraging the hiring of minorities, and Major League Baseball, which he suggested discriminated against players on religious grounds by reprimanding Christian players for writing Bible verses on their caps on Pride Night. The outcomes of those investigations remained unclear on Wednesday.

Last month, Mr. Uthmeier sent a letter to the Times Company making similar demands for the records. The company refused.

item.title: Judge Holds Off on Immediate Ruling on White House’s Media Ban
item.description:
A federal judge on Wednesday declined to issue an immediate ruling on the White House’s ban against CNN, MS NOW and Politico after hearing arguments from the two sides in the case, leaving the ban in place for the time being.

The judge, Timothy J. Kelly of U.S. District Court in Washington, appeared skeptical of the legality of the ban during the hearing. But he pulled up short of immediately reversing the ban, as the media outlets had asked. He instead said he would rule “as soon as possible.”

The ban dates to Friday, when President Trump declared in a Truth Social post that he would bar CNN, Politico and MS NOW from the White House because of their reporting. On Saturday, journalists for each outlet were denied access to White House grounds, and by Monday, the outlets had sued the administration, arguing the ban was a violation of their First Amendment rights.

Other media companies pulled back from their routine coverage of presidential events as a show of support for the banned outlets. The television pool — five networks that share the responsibility of providing and distributing television coverage of the president — suspended that coverage starting Monday. The New York Times and The Washington Post also limited publication of photos taken from the president’s events as part of a broader effort among journalists to boycott in support of the barred journalists. NPR stopped using audio from White House events, according to an internal memo viewed by The Times.

A lawyer for the media outlets, Theodore J. Boutrous, told the judge in Wednesday’s hearing that Mr. Trump’s repeated statements that he had imposed the ban because he took exception to journalism from certain media organizations made him “our lead witness.”

Mr. Boutrous said such a rationale infringes on the outlets’ constitutional rights. “He keeps proving our point,” Mr. Boutrous said.

Mr. Boutrous also responded to the White House’s argument, in court filings, that the ban stemmed from “reporting incidents” that threatened national security.

Judge Kelly asked Mr. Boutrous whether disclosing classified information that the White House viewed as endangering national security could justify revoking White House press credentials. Mr. Boutrous responded that such a move would be unconstitutional “viewpoint discrimination,” and would threaten the country’s tradition of uncompromising reporting on national security.

A lawyer for the administration, Michael Velchik, countered that the outlets were embracing an “absurd interpretation of the First Amendment.” He said the affected outlets mistakenly thought they could “knowingly publish classified information” while still enjoying “privileged access to the White House complex.” He argued that access to the White House is a “privilege, not a right.”

Mr. Velchik said that the three outlets had received notice of the ban and had been given an opportunity to challenge the White House’s decision. He was referring to letters that the White House sent to CNN, MS NOW and Politico on Tuesday, days after the outlets were denied access, describing the ban as “preliminary” and offering them until Friday to object.

Judge Kelly interrupted Mr. Velchik to question whether that notification constituted the sort of due process required before booting reporters out of the complex.

“I don’t know how a letter that they got after the pass was revoked could provide them with the kind of — the standard that they’d have to conform their conduct to,” said the judge.

In his rebuttal, Mr. Boutrous scoffed at the idea that the White House was offering the news outlets a bona fide opportunity to appeal the ban. “The president has made absolute clear he despises the reporting” of the banned news organizations, said Mr. Boutrous. “They’re going to keep playing games, they’re going to keep moving the ball.”

Judge Kelly also decided a similar case from November 2018, when Mr. Trump, in his first term, expelled CNN’s Jim Acosta from the White House complex. Mr. Acosta wasn’t given an opportunity to rebut his banishment, he said at the time.

At least one of the stories that the White House cited as failing to meet its standards was actually based on a press call organized by the White House itself. In its letter to Politico explaining the ban, the White House pointed to a June article from the outlet that said the odds of reaching a preliminary deal to end the Iran war were about 80 percent, “according to a senior administration official.” That senior administration official was speaking on a call organized and authorized by the White House, according to an invitation that was sent to The New York Times. The Times also attended and reported on the call at the time.

The Washington Post earlier reported on the origins of the June Politico article.

Fights over journalistic access have become a staple of Mr. Trump’s presidency. In his first term, the White House revoked another reporter’s access in addition to Mr. Acosta’s. Both recovered their credentials in legal proceedings.

At the start of his second term, Mr. Trump also booted The Associated Press from the pool of journalists who cover the president in such spaces as the Oval Office and Air Force One. That case remains in litigation.

Mr. Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has also imposed reporting and access restrictions on news organizations that have been successfully challenged in court by The Times; the Pentagon is appealing those rulings.

item.title: Major TV Networks Declined to Film Xi’s Arrival
item.description:
It could be remembered as a landmark moment in U.S.-China relations: the arrival on Wednesday evening of China’s top leader, Xi Jinping, in the United States, where he was greeted by President Trump at Joint Base Andrews.

But because of Mr. Trump’s continuing standoff with the White House press corps, no major network camera captured the proceedings.

Since Monday, the networks that operate the White House TV pool — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox News and NBC — have declined to film Mr. Trump’s public events as an act of solidarity with CNN, which, along with MS NOW and Politico, has been barred by the Trump administration.

Because of a quirk in timing, an unusual scene unfolded on the Andrews tarmac as reporters waited for Mr. Xi’s plane to land.

Crews from CBS, Fox News and NBC had set up their camera and audio equipment earlier in the afternoon, because a federal judge in Washington was hearing arguments in a lawsuit filed by the three banned outlets to restore their access to the White House.

If the judge had issued a ruling from the bench to suspend Mr. Trump’s press ban, and if the TV pool had decided to resume operations, the crews would have been ready to broadcast live footage of Mr. Xi.

But the judge, Timothy J. Kelly, declined to issue any order, saying he needed time to weigh his decision. So the network crews dismantled their equipment and departed before the Chinese leader arrived.

Some smaller TV networks were on-hand at Andrews, including One America News and the Right Side Broadcasting Network. LindellTV, a fledgling digital news site founded by Mike Lindell, the chief executive of MyPillow, was there as well.

The Associated Press captured video of Mr. Trump’s greeting of Mr. Xi and made the footage available to its subscribers, but the wire service said it would not stream the feed on its own platforms. “We continue to stand with our colleagues at other news organizations who have had their access restricted,” an A.P. spokesman said.

On Thursday, the president has a full day of high-stakes meetings with Mr. Xi. Usually, footage of a high-stakes summit of two global leaders would be scrutinized for every minute aspect of the leaders’ body language and interactions.

It remained unclear if Mr. Trump’s ban would still be in effect on Thursday, and how that might affect the networks’ coverage plans for the day’s events.

Katie Robertson contributed reporting.

item.title: Epstein’s Accountant and Lawyer Are Said to Be Under Federal Investigation
item.description:
Federal authorities in Manhattan have begun investigating some of the activities of Jeffrey Epstein’s longtime accountant and lawyer, who both serve as executors of the sex offender’s once vast estate, said two people who are familiar with the inquiry but not permitted to speak publicly.

Mr. Epstein’s longtime lawyer, Darren Indyke, and his accountant, Richard Kahn, have repeatedly denied any knowledge of their former employer’s sexual abuse of hundreds of teenage girls and young women.

It is unclear what the inquiry, which includes agents from the Federal Bureau of Investigation and federal prosecutors in New York, is focused on, the people said.

The Justice Department has been under pressure for years to more aggressively investigate some of Mr. Epstein’s associates, including people who may have enabled his sex trafficking. Some of his victims have denounced past announcements by federal authorities that the Epstein matter was essentially closed.

The release early this year of millions of emails and financial records obtained during federal investigations of Mr. Epstein fanned calls for prosecutors to take a fresh look to see if anyone should be charged with crimes.

The investigation of Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn was reported earlier by The Wall Street Journal.

Lawyers for Mr. Kahn and Mr. Indyke said in a statement that their clients had not been told “they are the subject or target of any investigation.”

The two men are “aware that the U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of New York recently asked to speak with at least one individual who provided services to Jeffrey Epstein,” the lawyers said. “But they do not have any information about the scope or focus of that investigation.”

The statement added, “Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn are confident that any investigation will reveal that they were not involved in any of Epstein’s crimes, just as the previous investigation found.”

Nicholas Biase, a spokesman for the U.S. attorney’s office, declined to comment.

The files released by the Justice Department and other court records show that Mr. Indyke and Mr. Kahn were heavily involved in wire transfers and cash withdrawals that went to some of the women whom Mr. Epstein is believed to have abused.

Both men denied any knowledge of Mr. Epstein’s crimes when they testified under oath this year before a congressional committee that has been investigating the Justice Department’s handling of the Epstein matter.

If there is money left in Mr. Epstein’s estate, Mr. Indyke stands to collect $50 million and Mr. Kahn $25 million, according to the terms of the will and a related trust that Mr. Epstein had drafted while in jail.

Federal authorities did not interview Mr. Indyke or Mr. Kahn after Mr. Epstein’s arrest and subsequent suicide in his Manhattan jail cell in 2019.

The only other person to be charged in connection with Mr. Epstein was his former girlfriend Ghislaine Maxwell. Ms. Maxwell was convicted in 2021 on charges that she helped recruit teenage girls for Mr. Epstein to sexually abuse. She is serving a 20-year prison sentence.

item.title: Elizabeth Holmes to Transfer to Halfway House in August 2027
item.description:
Elizabeth Holmes may be leaving prison early.

Ms. Holmes, the founder of the blood-testing start-up Theranos, who was convicted of fraud in 2022 and sentenced to 11 years behind bars, has been approved for transfer to a halfway house next August, according to copies of a Sept. 22 letter sent to victims of her crime from a unit manager within the Federal Bureau of Prisons. The letter was viewed by The New York Times.

Ms. Holmes, 42, is expected to transfer from F.P.C. Bryan, a minimum-security federal prison camp for women roughly 90 minutes northwest of Houston where she began her sentence in May 2023. She will move to the Austin Transitional Center in Del Valle, Texas, on Aug. 23, 2027, according to the letter.

ABC News reported earlier on the letters to Ms. Holmes’s victims.

It is unclear what prompted the transfer or how long Ms. Holmes may stay at the halfway house. The letter indicated that her scheduled release date is Feb. 22, 2030, though most prisoners stay in halfway houses only for a short time. Ms. Holmes’s sentence was already shortened several times. Last year, she filed a request to have her sentence commuted by the Department of Justice.

F.P.C. Bryan did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Holmes has been back in the spotlight in recent weeks with the upcoming release of a documentary directed by Nathan Fielder, a comedian, and Lance Oppenheim, called “You Can See Everything.”

Mr. Fielder spent time with Ms. Holmes and her partner, the tech worker Billy Evans, in the weeks before she reported to prison, keeping the project a secret until recently. The film’s distributor, A24, described the movie as “an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon” that became “a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.” It is set to be released on Oct. 16.

Mr. Evans declined to comment.

Ms. Holmes has also become active on social media while in prison, posting about artificial intelligence, longevity and the health care system and making the unfounded claim that Theranos’s technology worked. Her account describes her posts as “mostly my words, posted by others.”

John Carreyrou contributed reporting.
